description: Rutindo (Africa Beyond Earth) is an engineering and innovation team exploring how Africa's diverse landscapes can help us understand and study the Moon and Mars. We aim to use NASA satellite data, geological information and terrain analysis to identify and compare potential planetary analogue locations across A. We welcome programmers, engineers, Earth science enthusiasts, researchers and designers interested in space exploration and data-driven innovation.
summary:
There is no screening of places on Earth which share similar conditions to NASA’s environment for lunar and Martian explorations.

**Rutindo: Africa Planetary Analogue Explorer** (https://rutindo.netlify.app/) is an interactive Geographic Information System (GIS) platform for evaluation of 652 African 2° grids across eight aspects of environment and terrain. Two types of assessment criteria are applied: rankings by relative percentiles in Africa and similarity score between 0 and 1 with respect to lunar and Martian reference standards.

Monte Carlo weight sensitivity analysis suggests robust rankings with rank correlation medians of 0.988-0.997. Saharan places head the Mars analogue screening in terms of absolute matching with the highest matching at 0.49, while Tibesti and Atacama have 0.47 and 0.42 matching correspondingly.

A detailed analysis of 0.25° Uganda grid of 285 squares indicates Rwenzori (0.24) and Mount Elgon (0.20) to be more promising sites for rugged terrain and cold altitude testing than deserts.

Rutindo gives preliminary screening results, not planetary equivalence proof.
details:
THE PROBLEM AND AFRICAN ANALOGUE GAP

Planetary field analogues for Moon and Mars exploration rely heavily on sites outside Africa, including the Atacama Desert, Iceland, and Utah. Yet Africa contains hyper-arid deserts, volcanic basalt fields, rift valleys, and high mountains that have not been systematically screened side by side. Single-score maps can also mislead mission planners by hiding important physical differences: a rugged mountain site, for example, is not automatically a Mars climate analogue.

HOW IT WORKS: DUAL SCORING AND SENSITIVITY CHECK

• Continental grid: Evaluates 1,295 two-degree grid boxes across Africa, retaining 652 land-qualified cells (at least 30% land). Eight variables are assessed: daytime heat extremes, nighttime cold extremes, elevation, local relief, rainfall, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), dust aerosol proxy, and bare-ground mafic index. The mafic index is considered reliable only where NDVI is below 0.25, leaving 285 eligible cells.

• Relative ranks (0–1): Ranks African locations by suitability for three mission presets: Mars-like aridity and dust, cold-soak and freeze-thaw, and lunar-like basalt.

• Absolute similarity (0–1): Compares locations directly against selected lunar and Martian surface reference benchmarks.

• Sensitivity check: Monte Carlo weight perturbation produces median rank correlations of 0.988–0.997 across the presets. This indicates stable rankings under weight changes, not physical validation.

• Tools & Stack: Built with Python (Google Earth Engine / Kaggle data pipeline), HTML5, CSS3, SVG/Canvas GIS rendering, and hosted live on Netlify.

KEY SCREENING FINDINGS

• Mars analogue screening: Saharan cell +24.0N, −16.0E achieves the highest reported absolute similarity score of 0.486, exceeding the Tibesti benchmark (0.471) and Atacama benchmark (0.422). Cell +22.0N, 16.0E leads the relative aridity and dust ranking (0.96), making it a potential location for rover mobility and dust-sealing tests.

• Lunar analogue screening: The Horn of Africa basaltic candidate (+10.0N, 48.0E) scores 0.363 in absolute similarity, while Egypt's Red Sea Hills (+24.0N, 34.0E) score 0.87 in the relative ranking. These are potential proxies for selected basalt-related instrument tests, not complete lunar analogues. No African candidate reproduces lunar south-polar temperatures (approximately −233 °C) or vacuum conditions.

• Uganda high-resolution screening: A separate 0.25-degree analysis of 285 Uganda grid boxes identifies the Rwenzori (+0.25N, 29.75E; 3,589 m elevation, 2,791 m relief, 0.66 °C cold nights) and Mount Elgon (+1.00N, 34.50E; 3,316 m elevation, 2,210 m relief, 0.60 °C cold nights) as potential rugged-terrain and cold-altitude test locations. Their reported cold-soak scores are 0.889 and 0.823, respectively. Katwe-Kikorongo (+0.00N, 29.75E) records the highest reported local relief (2,879 m). Uganda's maximum reported Mars similarity score is 0.237, suggesting greater potential for operational terrain testing than for desert climate simulation.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Rutindo provides preliminary screening evidence, not confirmed planetary equivalence. African environments cannot reproduce the near-vacuum conditions of the Moon or the low atmospheric pressure and extreme cold of Mars. Candidate locations have not yet been ground-truthed. Next steps include checking basaltic candidates against orbital geological maps, installing environmental loggers at three to five priority locations, and conducting rover slope-mobility and cold-soak trials in Uganda.
